generatedProse.concept-context: Across disciplines, practice and work-based learning is usually assessed through a reflective account or log, not through the activity itself. Tutors and supervisors are guided by the standards of the field. They look for evidence that you can reflect on your own practice: what a task revealed about how you work, how it connects to what you have studied, and what you will change. The account is the thing that is marked.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who submit a reflective account of the same placement.

Student A writes a clear, orderly account of what the placement involved: the setting, the daily routine, the tasks observed. It reads well and is accurate. But it is a description. It tells the assessor what happened and little about what Student A learned, so almost nothing can be credited as reflection or insight.

Student B writes less about the routine and more about what it revealed. Student B describes one task that went wrong, reflects on the part played in it, links it to a standard or idea studied beforehand, and sets out what is now done differently and why. The account shows evidenced insight into one's own practice. That is what the criteria reward.

Both students did the same placement and wrote to the same length. Only Student B articulated the learning, which is what is actually assessed.
generatedProse.summary: Practice and work-based learning is assessed through reflection because every setting differs: what is marked is the learning you articulate, not the activity itself. A strong reflective account moves beyond description to evidenced insight, honest reflection, a link to what you have studied, and a specific change you will make. You can now explain how this learning is assessed, articulate your own learning, and judge an account against what assessors look for. You can turn any experience into learning you can show.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Student B's account stronger than Student A's?

items.text: It showed evidenced insight into the student's own learning, not just a description of events.
It described the placement in more detail.
It was written more clearly and was better organised.
It was longer than Student A's account.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B's account showed evidenced insight into the student's own learning.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B's account showed beyond a description of events.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B's account was stronger because it showed evidenced insight into the learning. Detail, clarity and length were not the difference.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
